author: William Saville
reader_character: Jasper — adult first-person protagonist, externally they/them
title: A Day of Ordinary Things
subtitle: Lanternweald — sixth expansion pass
content:
Maui ruined the laundry.

Not all of it. Just my favorite shirt, which had once been blue and now looked like something rescued from the bottom of a teapot.

I held it up between two fingers.

"What happened?"

He glanced at the washing tub.

"Alchemical incident."

"Did you put the red cloth in with everything else?"

"It was a small red cloth."

"That isn't a defense."

"It was very small."

I started laughing. I was too tired to be properly angry, and the sight of the mighty Maui trying to explain how a single handkerchief had defeated him was impossible to resist.

He looked relieved.

"You're not furious?"

"I liked that shirt."

"I'll get you another."

"Maybe. But I want to know how to avoid this happening again."

He looked toward the washing line.

"Separate the red cloth?"

"Now you're learning."

The day had been set aside for doing nothing useful.

We were terrible at it.

Maui began by deciding the kitchen shelves needed rearranging. I found three misplaced cups, two jars of rosemary, and a spoon that had apparently been living behind the flour for several weeks. Then I offered to measure a new hook for the pantry door and wrote down the wrong number twice.

Mara saw the sketch.

"Are you building a hook for a giant?" she asked.

"Possibly."

She held the ruler against the actual door and smiled.

"Try again."

I did.

We returned to Tideglass with the corrected measurement and a bag of bread. On the way, Lio called from the skiff, where the new seat needed sanding.

Maui took one step toward the landing.

I caught his hand.

"Not today."

He stopped.

"I was only going to look."

"You were going to fix."

"Perhaps."

"Lio has Fen."

He sighed dramatically, then waved instead.

Lio waved back and returned to the work.

We had lunch on the porch, where the wind moved through the hanging lantern hooks and the sea made its ordinary music below. Maui told me a story from his homeworld that did not involve a triumph. It involved an elderly fisherman, a stubborn basket, and a lesson about not borrowing tools without returning them.

"Did you return the basket?" I asked.

"Eventually."

"Before or after you broke it?"

He stared into his soup.

I laughed again.

In the afternoon we tried to repair the loose shutter by the bedroom window. I measured the hinge spacing incorrectly. Maui drilled the first hole too close to the edge. We stood looking at the damage.

"Well," he said.

"Well."

"I could make a new shutter."

"Or we could ask Tamsin what kind of patch will hold."

He nodded.

We wrote a note rather than pretending the mistake hadn't happened.

At dusk, I made dinner. The soup was too salty. The bread had cooled. Maui burned his fingers trying to take a pan off the stove without a cloth.

I put a cool wet towel in his hand.

"You're a disaster," I told him.

"Yet you're still here."

"Very concerning, isn't it?"

He smiled, but a small hesitation crossed his face.

I set down the towel.

"What?"

He looked away.

"Sometimes I think you're going to get tired of how often I need to learn things that everyone else already knows."

I sat beside him.

"I learn things all the time."

"You don't make them into public disasters."

"Ask Mara about the hook measurement."

"That's different."

"Why?"

He struggled for an answer.

I watched the kitchen light move over his face. He had spent so long being expected to save people that the ordinary incompetence of living with someone seemed almost unbearable.

"Listen," I said. "I don't need you to be perfect. I need you to admit when something went wrong, help repair it, and let me do the same."

He looked at the pink shirt hanging by the stove.

"Even when the laundry is a tragedy?"

"Especially then."

He took my hand.

"Can I keep trying?"

"Yes."

He leaned toward me, slow enough for me to meet him. I kissed him, tasting the faint edge of burnt bread and hearing his laugh when I pulled away.

"Romantic," he murmured.

"Ridiculous."

"Both."

We ate the salty soup anyway.

Later, we carried the dishes to the sink and left them soaking. The shutter would wait until Tamsin could look at it. The laundry would be washed separately next time. The kitchen would probably never be fully organized, and nobody would award us a medal for surviving an ordinary day.

I found a small blue thread still clinging to Maui's sleeve.

I pulled it free.

He looked at me.

"What?"

"Nothing. Just proof you actually did the laundry."

"I did."

"Badly."

"Heroically badly."

I laughed and leaned against him.

The moon was bright over Tideglass. The lower landing glimmered with wet stones, and the upper path lanterns burned quietly. Tomorrow there would be meetings and repairs and people who needed help.

Tonight there was a pink shirt, a crooked shutter, and the warm breath of someone who wanted to keep learning how to live with me.

I wrote the day in my green notebook.

Not *we accomplished nothing.*

Instead: *We made mistakes, and the house is still home.*
